title: How do you use the profitability framework when a client's profits fall?
description: "How can the client make more profit?" Profits are falling, or the client wants them higher.
hook: When a client's profits fall, use the profitability framework to split profit into revenue and costs, find which side moved, then drill down until you reach the cause behind the number. Start by asking whether revenue, costs or both changed, and whether the whole industry is affected or just your client. Here is the tree, how to adapt it, and a short worked example.
body:
When you will use it

Use it whenever profits are falling or the client wants them higher, and as the backbone of revenue decline cases. It is a diagnose question: "why is this happening, and how do we fix it?" You break profit into parts that add up, find the part that moved, then fix that part. See which framework to use for each type of question for the other families.

Ask this first

Is it revenue, costs or both? And is the whole industry seeing this, or just our client?

The first half tells you which branch to open. The second tells you whether the cause is in the market (a demand slump, a new rival, rising input prices for everyone) or inside the company (a pricing mistake, a failing channel, waste).

The structure

  • Revenue = units sold × price per unit
    • Units: number of customers × purchases per customer
    • Price: list price, discounts, product mix
  • Costs
    • Fixed costs: rent, salaried staff, overheads
    • Variable costs: materials, delivery, commissions

Fixed and variable matter because they behave differently when volume falls. If most costs are fixed, a small drop in sales causes a large drop in profit. Our explainer on operating leverage shows the maths.

Make it your own

A bare "revenue and costs" tree will not impress anyone. Two moves make it specific:

  • Segment every line. Split by product, customer group, channel and region. A shift in mix often hides inside an average: a retailer's average basket can fall because more sales come from a cheaper online range, even though no price changed.
  • Use the client's own drivers. For an airline, units are seats flown × load factor. For a gym, they are members × months. For a software firm, customers × revenue per customer. Name the branches in those terms.

A short worked example

A regional retailer's revenue was $12M in both years, but profit fell from $1.8M to $1.2M. The figures are illustrative.

Split the change. Revenue is flat, so the $0.6M fall sits in costs, which rose from $10.2M to $10.8M.

Find the driver. Ask for a cost bridge:

Cost lineChangeShare of the rise
Freight+$350k58%
Wages+$200k33%
Utilities+$50k8%
Total+$600k100%

Ask why. Freight explains most of the change, so the next question is not "how can we cut costs?" It is "did the cost per delivery rise, or the number of deliveries?" Suppose orders were flat but more customers chose home delivery: deliveries rose from 50,000 to 85,000 at about $10 each, which is 35,000 × $10 = $350k. Same sales, more expensive to serve.

Fix the economics. A $4 charge on home deliveries would raise about 85,000 × $4 = $340k if volumes held, recovering most of the freight rise. Other options are a minimum basket for free delivery or denser delivery routes. Check that the fix does not just push cost onto another line or drive customers to rivals.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer jumps to ideas:

To raise profits they could increase prices, cut costs, and look for new customers.

A strong answer locates the problem before fixing it:

Revenue is flat, so the whole $600k sits in costs. Freight explains almost 60% of it, so I'd like to know whether that's more deliveries or a higher cost per delivery.

The mistakes to avoid

  1. Fixing before diagnosing. Check which side moved, and whether the industry is affected, before suggesting anything.
  2. Stopping at the accounting line. "Freight went up" is a symptom. "Customers switched to home delivery" is the cause.
  3. Ignoring mix. Averages hide shifts between products, channels and customers.
  4. Cutting costs that earn revenue. A fix that loses customers can leave profit lower than before.

Practise with real prompts

1. A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show the answer
  • Market: total applications across lenders, driven by rates, house prices and transactions. Is everyone down 20%?
  • Our offer: rates and fees against rivals, loan-to-value limits, product range.
  • Channels and process: are brokers placing fewer loans with us? Time to decision, approval rates, drop-off.

Where to start: the market. If all banks are down 20%, the client's share has not changed.

The trap: jumping to marketing ideas before checking whether the whole market fell.

2. A ski resort's profits fell 40% after two warm winters.

Show the answer
  • Winter revenue: visitors × spend, by month; lift passes, ski school, food, rentals.
  • Costs: mostly fixed (lifts, staff, maintenance), plus snowmaking and energy.
  • Snow risk: days open, altitude, snowmaking coverage; trend or two bad years?
  • Non-ski income: summer, events, conferences.

Where to start: days open. Warm winters cut the season while costs stay fixed.

The trap: missing that weather is the root cause.

3. A cinema chain's attendance is still 25% below pre-pandemic levels.

Show the answer
  • Market: total cinema attendance against ours; the supply of big releases.
  • Our offer: ticket and snack prices, comfort, screens, locations.
  • Substitutes: shorter gaps before films reach streaming; home viewing habits.
  • Customers: which groups have not come back; fewer visitors or fewer visits each?

Where to start: market against us. Are we below the industry, or is the whole market smaller?

The trap: ignoring the supply of films, which drives much of attendance.
